ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.rationale: Recent immobilization or prior VTE/malignancy increases the likelihood of DVT and changes the urgency of imaging.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

ask.changes_what: Positive: trial withdrawal/dose reduction and reassess, check creatinine; negative or non-resolving: pursue HF, venous, renal, hepatic and DVT causes.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not label edema as drug-induced when there is dyspnea, orthopnea, elevated JVP, unilateral swelling, hypoalbuminemia/proteinuria or rising creatinine until those causes are evaluated.
ask.escalation_warning: Thiazolidinedione- or NSAID-associated edema with weight gain and dyspnea may be new/worsened heart failure; NSAID edema with oliguria or rising creatinine indicates AKI - stop the drug and assess urgently.
ask.how: Review the full list for dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine), NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, pregabalin/gabapentin, corticosteroids, direct vasodilators (minoxidil, hydralazine), estrogens/progestins, testosterone, docetaxel, and DPP-4 or insulin. Record start date and dose escalation relative to edema onset and whether edema is bilateral, dependent and non-tender.
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug makes medication effect unlikely and directs evaluation toward heart failure, venous insufficiency, renal/hepatic disease or DVT (if unilateral).
ask.pitfalls: Up to one-third of edema on amlodipine is not caused by it, and thiazolidinediones/NSAIDs can precipitate true heart failure rather than benign edema; drug edema is a diagnosis of exclusion when JVP, BNP or echo suggest cardiac disease. Unilateral or painful edema is never attributed to medication.
ask.positive_finding: Bilateral dependent edema beginning weeks after starting or increasing a dihydropyridine CCB, NSAID, thiazolidinedione, gabapentinoid, steroid or vasodilator, without orthopnea, elevated JVP or weight gain out of proportion, supports drug-induced edema (and NSAIDs also cause AKI/sodium retention).
ask.prerequisites: Reconciled medication list including over-the-counter NSAIDs; weight trend, orthopnea/PND and JVP assessment to distinguish drug edema from heart failure.
ask.rationale: Certain medications can cause or worsen edema, and identifying them may change management if DVT is less likely.
ask.title: Medication review for edema: dihydropyridine CCB, NSAIDs, thiazolidinediones, pregabalin/gabapentin, steroids, minoxidil/hydralazine

examine.changes_what: Positive: adds 1 Wells point and pushes toward compression ultrasound; negative does not stop work-up if other Wells items or D-dimer are positive.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm calf compression if DVT is strongly suspected and pain is severe.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a negative calf measurement to withhold imaging in a patient with moderate/high Wells probability or with symptoms suggesting PE.
examine.escalation_warning: Massive swelling with cyanosis or pallor and pain (phlegmasia) or a cold pulseless limb requires immediate vascular imaging and consultation.

examine.how: With the patient supine and legs relaxed, mark a point 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity on each leg and measure calf circumference with a tape at the same level bilaterally. A difference >3 cm (symptomatic side larger) is positive; also note localized tenderness along the deep venous system and pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg.
examine.negative_finding: No calf-diameter difference (LR- 0.57) or no calf swelling (LR- 0.67) lowers the probability of DVT only modestly; it cannot exclude DVT on its own.
examine.pitfalls: Chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema, cellulitis, Baker cyst, and prior DVT produce asymmetry without acute thrombosis; measuring at different levels or in a dependent leg creates spurious differences. Calf tenderness alone has LR near 1.
examine.positive_finding: Calf-diameter difference roughly doubles the odds of DVT (pooled LR+ 1.8); it is the only physical sign with useful rule-in value but is far weaker than the overall Wells score (high probability LR 5.2).
examine.prerequisites: Both legs accessible and comparable (no prior amputation, cast, or chronic unilateral disease that already explains asymmetry).
examine.rationale: A significant difference in calf circumference supports DVT and increases the need for urgent imaging.
examine.title: Unilateral leg swelling: calf circumference difference >3 cm (10 cm below tibial tuberosity), with calf tenderness

examine.changes_what: Unilateral warm erythema: treat as cellulitis but rule out DVT/necrotizing infection; bilateral: seek pseudocellulitis (stasis, dermatitis) before antibiotics.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use asymmetry/border to reassure when there is severe pain, rapid progression, bullae, crepitus, hypotension or immunocompromise; necrotizing infection needs surgical evaluation regardless of score.
examine.escalation_warning: Unilateral swollen warm leg also fits DVT: obtain compression ultrasound if no clear portal of entry or if edema dominates over erythema.

examine.how: Expose and compare both legs. Note whether erythema is unilateral (asymmetric) or bilateral, feel for warmth with the back of the hand against the contralateral limb, and trace the border (marking it with pen for follow-up). Check for a portal of entry (tinea, ulcer), tenderness, and disproportionate pain, crepitus or bullae.
examine.negative_finding: Bilateral symmetric erythema without fever, leukocytosis or tachycardia favors stasis dermatitis or other pseudocellulitis (ALT-70 0-2 points: >=83% pseudocellulitis); bilateral cellulitis is rare.
examine.pitfalls: ALT-70 is sensitive but only 22% specific in a prospective ED validation, so a 'positive' asymmetric leg still includes many DVT, gout, contact dermatitis and stasis cases; warmth is subjective; do not miss necrotizing infection (pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus).
examine.positive_finding: Unilateral warm, tender erythema, especially with leukocytosis, tachycardia or age >=70 (ALT-70 >=5 points), gives >=82% likelihood of true cellulitis in the derivation cohort. Asymmetry is the heaviest-weighted item (3 points).
examine.prerequisites: Both legs exposed; heart rate, temperature and WBC available if scoring ALT-70.
examine.rationale: Warmth and erythema with a defined border suggest cellulitis, which is a key alternative diagnosis to DVT.
examine.title: Unilateral warm erythema with defined border (vs bilateral / stasis change)

examine.changes_what: Bilateral pitting edema plus elevated JVP should shift dyspnea toward HF and prompt BNP/echo; unilateral edema should trigger DVT evaluation instead.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid pressing over cellulitis, ulcers or a suspected DVT.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on edema alone to diagnose or exclude HF, or to judge acute volume status in a hypotensive or oliguric patient.
examine.escalation_warning: Unilateral painful edema needs DVT evaluation; rapidly progressive bilateral edema with hypotension or rising creatinine suggests cardiorenal or cirrhotic decompensation and needs urgent assessment.

evidence.citation: Mant J, Doust J, Roalfe A, et al. Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of diagnosis of heart failure, with modelling of implications of different diagnostic strategies in primary care. Health Technol Assess. 2009;13(32):1-207.
evidence.population: Individual patient data from 9 studies of adults with suspected heart failure (predominantly primary care / open-access referral cohorts)
evidence.quote: oedema (72%) ... sensitivity of these features was low, ranging from 11% (added heart sounds) to 53% (oedema)
evidence.reference_standard: Heart failure diagnosis by echocardiography-based criteria of each included study
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (any) in patients with suspected heart failure

examine.how: Press firmly with the thumb for at least 5 s over the dorsum of the foot, behind the medial malleolus and over the tibial shaft, then release. Note whether a pit persists (pitting), its depth and duration (grade 1-4), how high up the leg it extends, and whether it is symmetric. Non-pitting, firm (brawny) edema suggests lymphedema or chronic venous disease.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of edema does not exclude heart failure (pooled sensitivity ~50%); acute HF and HFpEF often present without edema.
examine.pitfalls: Dependent edema in chronically seated or elderly patients is common without HF; edema lags behind volume changes by days, so it tracks chronic rather than acute volume status.
examine.positive_finding: Bilateral pitting edema modestly raises the probability of heart failure in dyspneic patients but is nonspecific: venous insufficiency, drugs, hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis produce the same sign. Unilateral edema points to a local cause (DVT, venous obstruction, cellulitis); brawny non-pitting edema suggests lymphedema.
examine.prerequisites: Compare both legs at the same level; ask about duration, leg dependency, and new drugs (calcium-channel blockers, thiazolidinediones, NSAIDs).
examine.rationale: Characterizing the edema as pitting and unilateral helps distinguish DVT from other causes like venous insufficiency or lymphedema.
examine.title: Lower-extremity edema: bilateral vs unilateral, pitting vs non-pitting (brawny), grade and level
